sections.heading: Giving my whole self to Christ
sections.text: Lord Jesus, you are true God, eternal life, and the Redeemer of sinners. I bring myself to you without holding anything back—my body, my soul, my mind, my choices, and my loves. Everything I have and everything I am belongs to you.
theological_themes: Christ is fully divine and the source of life.
A servant of Christ offers the whole person to him, not only public work or religious activity.
Christian ministry begins with belonging to Christ before doing anything for Christ.

scripture_references.connection: Thomas confesses the risen Jesus as Lord and God, grounding the prayer’s direct worship of Christ as truly divine.
Paul urges believers to present their bodies to God as living sacrifices, which supports the prayer’s total consecration of body, mind, will, and affections.

sections.heading: Coming to you for rest from guilt and eternity
sections.text: I come to you because I need rest deep down in my soul. My guilt is too loud for me to silence, and eternity is too serious for me to ignore. Let the ordinary things around me—this day, this world, my home, my table, my books, my food, and my clothes—stand as witnesses that I am not pretending to be self-sufficient. I am coming to you because only you can give me peace.
theological_themes: Human guilt before God is real and cannot be managed by self-reliance.
Christ invites burdened sinners to come to him for rest.
Daily, ordinary life can become the setting for honest covenantal surrender to God.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus calls the weary and burdened to come to him for rest, which directly supports the prayer’s movement from guilt and dread toward Christ as the soul’s refuge.
This passage treats death and judgment as realities every person must face, giving weight to the prayer’s seriousness about eternity.

sections.heading: Asking for a real heart, not an empty appearance
sections.text: Give me a heart that has been changed by you, so that I love you from the inside out. Give me a clean and steady spirit that wants your glory more than my own. Put in me the kind of life you recognize as your own work. Give me a true share in the blood that cleanses, the righteousness that makes sinners right with God, and the redemption that sets captives free. Please do not let me fool myself, serve in your name outwardly, and then be exposed as false when I stand before you.
theological_themes: True religion requires inward renewal, not merely outward office or appearance.
Salvation rests on Christ’s cleansing blood, justifying righteousness, and redeeming work.
Fear of hypocrisy before final judgment leads to humble dependence on grace.

scripture_references.connection: God promises to circumcise the heart so his people will love him, which illuminates the prayer’s request for inward renewal that produces real love for God.
John connects fellowship with God to the cleansing power of Jesus’ blood, supporting the prayer’s appeal to Christ’s blood as the answer to guilt and uncleanness.
Paul holds together redemption, Christ’s blood, and justification by grace, matching the prayer’s confidence in Christ’s saving work rather than personal merit.
Jesus warns that some who appear religious and active in his name will be rejected as unknown to him, grounding the prayer’s fear of being a hypocrite at judgment.

sections.heading: Consecrating my ministry and asking to be kept from bringing harm
sections.text: Because of your death for me, take my time, my energy, my abilities, my usefulness, and even the parts of my life that look most spiritual. I set them apart for you with a sincere heart. Keep sin from settling in me and clouding my sight. Keep foolishness from drying up the gifts you have given. Protect me from the kinds of falls that have damaged others, so that your name is not dishonored, your people are not wounded, those who oppose you are not strengthened in their unbelief, and my own conscience is not wrecked.
theological_themes: Christ’s sacrificial death calls for wholehearted consecration in service.
Ministry gifts can be damaged by sin, pride, and folly.
A leader’s sin can dishonor Christ, grieve the church, harden opponents, and wound the servant’s own peace.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that Christ’s death compels believers to live no longer for themselves but for him, which undergirds the prayer’s offering of time, strength, and gifts to Christ.
Paul tells Timothy to keep close watch on both himself and his teaching, showing why a minister must guard personal holiness as well as public service.
Paul urges usefulness to the Master through cleansing from dishonorable things and fleeing youthful passions, closely fitting the prayer’s concern that sin not wither gifts or ruin service.

sections.heading: Learning the truth about myself now
sections.text: Fill my heart with love for you and for people. And please show me, while there is still time to repent, what I really am before you. Do not let me live under a false idea of myself and only discover the truth when this life is over.
theological_themes: Love for God and neighbor is central to faithful service.
Self-examination before God is mercy when it leads to repentance now rather than exposure later.
A minister needs truth about the heart, not merely usefulness in public.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus identifies love for God and neighbor as the heart of the law, supporting the prayer’s request for love toward Christ and others.
The psalmist asks God to search and expose the heart in order to be led rightly, which fits the prayer’s desire to know the truth about oneself before God now.
Paul calls professing believers to examine themselves, grounding the prayer’s concern not to live with a false spiritual identity.

sections.heading: Preparing me to die in peace
sections.text: Prepare me for death. I ask, if it pleases you, that my last days would not be dragged out in long distress or come with sudden confusion, but that you would give me a clear and peaceful departure. Let me be able to say goodbye to your people well. Do not let me simply be left in the world like unused timber in a house. When my work is done, quietly move me from this world into the next, held by you.
theological_themes: Christians may honestly ask God for a peaceful death while submitting the timing and manner to his will.
Death is not the end for those who belong to Christ, but a departure to be with him.
A servant of God wants to be useful until the Lord’s appointed removal.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes death for the believer as gain and as departing to be with Christ, which supports the prayer’s hope of being moved from this world into the next.
Paul speaks of his death as a departure after completing his course, illuminating the prayer’s desire to finish faithfully and leave in peace when the work is done.
Moses asks God to teach his people to number their days wisely, fitting the prayer’s desire to live and die with spiritual readiness.

sections.heading: Asking you to carry this covenant to the Father
sections.text: Lord Jesus, take these requests and make them yours before the Father. Put your own yes over what is truly according to your will. I put my yes here too: I belong to you, I need you, and I give myself to you again.
theological_themes: Christ intercedes for his people before the Father.
Prayer is offered with confidence through Christ, not through personal worthiness.
Covenant renewal includes both dependence on Christ and willing self-offering to him.

scripture_references.connection: Hebrews teaches that Jesus is able to save completely because he always lives to intercede, grounding the prayer’s request that Christ present these petitions to the Father.
Paul says God’s promises find their Yes in Christ, which supports the prayer’s appeal for Christ’s own Amen over what accords with God’s will.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original asks for a particular manner of death: neither after long affliction nor suddenly, but after a short illness with an orderly farewell. That reflects a historical Christian concern for dying consciously and peacefully, but it needed to be framed as a request submitted to God’s will rather than a guaranteed or superior form of death.

The prayer’s fear of being found a hypocrite on Judgment Day is intentionally severe. I preserved that force rather than softening it into general anxiety, while grounding it in biblical warnings about false profession.

The original is specifically ministerial, and assumes the public consequences of a minister’s sin for Christ’s name, the church, outsiders, and personal peace. I retained that focus rather than generalizing it into ordinary private discipleship.
significant_interpretive_choices: I rendered the long list of created and household objects as the ordinary surroundings of life bearing witness to the speaker’s surrender, rather than reproducing every item in the same rhythm. This preserves the concrete covenant-witness image without archaic formality.
I interpreted “a principle within which thou wilt own” as a genuine inward work of grace that Christ recognizes as his own, rather than as a vague moral impulse.

I treated “interest in the blood… righteousness… redemption” as a true saving share in Christ’s cleansing, justifying, and liberating work, using contemporary wording while keeping the theological sequence intact.
I adapted “Let not my days end like lumber in a house” as a request not to remain uselessly in the world after one’s work is done, preserving the image of unused timber without making it obscure.
